body:
We Are Still Writing the Response

Tisha B’Av · Edus · Shema · Nachamu

I. The Day After

Here we are, Erev Shabbos Va'eschanan. Yesterday was Tisha B'Av. Tisha B'Av is hard. There is no other way to put it.

Going into the fast this year, there was still that thought, perhaps that we were coming down to the final seconds. Maybe Mashiach would come, Tisha B'Av would be transformed, the sackcloth and mourning would be pulled away. We are ready for that. We want that. We want to sit down to a seudah rather than continue mourning. Yet Tisha B'Av arrived, and once again we sat on the floor.

When we think about Tisha B'Av, we think about destruction, death, and all the different expressions of mourning. But there is also a personal question worth sitting with: how do events that occurred thousands of years ago become emotionally real to us? For many people, myself included, it can be genuinely difficult to bridge the historical distance separating us from the original Churban. We can read Eichah. We can say the Kinnos. We can learn the accounts of what happened. But emotionally, we are very far removed.

What I find easier to connect to is the future. Mashiach is coming. The third Beis HaMikdash will be built. Hashem's presence will once again be clearly visible and felt throughout the world. That is exciting. And it is easier for me to feel the pain of not having that reality yet than to feel the original flames of the Churban. The event is ancient, but the absence is current. We still do not have what we are waiting for. We are still waiting.

II. Can We Yet Deliver the Hesped?

The Kinnos help us bridge generations. Many were composed centuries ago. Some reach back more than a thousand years. Yet Jewish communities have continued adding Kinnos for later tragedies, the Shoah, the expulsions, the pogroms. In our kehillah, we also read a Kinah written in response to the attacks of October 7.

Before each Kinah, someone gives an introduction. Before this one, the speaker raised a powerful point about a hesped. A hesped is normally delivered as a person is about to be buried. The death is final. The reality has changed. The hesped begins the painful process of confronting that finality and moving toward some measure of closure.

But what happened to Klal Yisrael on October 7 has not reached its conclusion. The war and its consequences remain active. Our enemies continue trying to harm us. Families continue living with unbearable loss. Klal Yisrael remains inside the story. Perhaps, then, we cannot yet deliver a hesped that treats October 7 as a completed chapter. The response cannot be only retrospective. It must still be a call to action. What must change within us? What are we being asked to learn? What are we going to build? We are not yet closing the book. We are still writing the Jewish response.

III. Moshe Speaks to the Next Generation

This leads directly into Sefer Devarim and into this week's parsha. Last week, we spoke about Devarim as Moshe Rabbeinu's final series of teachings to the generation preparing to enter Eretz Yisrael. Some members of that generation had lived through earlier events. Others had been born in the Midbar. Yet all of them needed to hear about what had happened to their parents.

Something great was awaiting them. They were about to enter the Land. Precisely because they were moving forward, they needed to understand what had come before. Moshe was not retelling the past so that they would remain trapped inside it. He was teaching them the past so that they could build a different future. That is the purpose of Jewish memory. We do not remember merely to look backward. We remember so that the next generation will know how to move forward.

IV. With Us, Those Who Are Alive Today

Va'eschanan contains some of the most powerful foundations of Jewish existence: the Aseres HaDibros and Shema. Before repeating the Aseres HaDibros, Moshe tells the people:

לֹא אֶת אֲבֹתֵינוּ כָּרַת הִ אֶת הַבְּרִית הַזֹּאת כִּי אִתָּנוּ אֲנַחְנוּ אֵלֶּה פֹה הַיּוֹם כֻּלָּנוּ חַיִּים

"Hashem did not make this covenant with our fathers alone, but with us, those of us who are here alive today."

— Devarim 5:3

Yet not every person listening to Moshe had physically stood at Har Sinai. Many had been born during the forty years in the wilderness. Why, then, does Moshe speak as though they had all been there? Because Har Sinai is not merely an event that happened to our ancestors. It is the foundational experience of Klal Yisrael. A later generation does not stand outside the covenant simply because its members were not yet born. Every Jewish generation receives the Torah anew. Every Jewish generation must hear Hashem speaking to it.

The people at Sinai experienced Hashem's revelation so intensely that they begged Moshe to receive the remainder on their behalf. They feared they could not survive the direct encounter. And yet that experience belongs to us. We were not physically standing beneath the mountain, but we inherit the covenant, the memory, and the responsibility.

V. Instruction and Experience: The Three Categories

At the beginning of the parsha, Moshe says:

וְעַתָּה יִשְׂרָאֵל שְׁמַע אֶל הַחֻקִּים וְאֶל הַמִּשְׁפָּטִים אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְלַמֵּד אֶתְכֶם

"And now, Israel, listen to the chukim and the mishpatim that I teach you to perform."

— Devarim 4:1

Notice what Moshe specifically says he is teaching: the chukim and the mishpatim. Mishpatim are laws whose justice human beings can often understand, prohibitions against murder, theft, harming others. Chukim are Divine statutes whose complete reasons remain beyond us, even when our teachers help us discover meaning within them. But edus, testimony, is not mentioned in that statement about teaching. And that omission matters.

Edus cannot be transmitted through instruction alone. Testimony points to something that happened, something that was encountered, and something that continues to define us. A teacher can explain the laws connected to an event. But for that event to become part of a person's identity, it must become experiential. A child can be told that Har Sinai occurred. But for Har Sinai to become part of that child's identity, the child must see that Torah is alive. A child can be taught the laws of Tisha B'Av. But for the Churban to become real, the child must experience a home and community that genuinely feel Hashem's absence and yearn for His return.

That is why parents, local rabbanim, teachers, and communities matter so deeply. Their responsibility is not merely to deliver information. They must take the eternal edus of Torah and make it a living experience within their own place, time, and circumstances. They must help their students encounter Har Sinai here. They must help their children feel Tisha B'Av now. They must show the next generation that Shema is not merely something we recite. It is the reality within which a Jew lives.

VI. Living Shema

Shema Yisrael, Hashem Elokeinu, Hashem Echad. This is the ultimate declaration of a Jew.

שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל הִ אֱלֹקֵינוּ הִ אֶחָד

"Hear, O Israel: Hashem is our God, Hashem is One."

— Devarim 6:4

We say Shema. We try to feel Shema. We are supposed to live within Shema. But what does that actually mean? As the Sforno explains, the ultimate purpose toward which all of history moves is the universal recognition of Hashem's unity. Everything will ultimately arrive at the truth that Hashem is One. That means it is not ultimately about me. It means that every fragmented piece of reality, including my pain, my responsibility, the suffering of another Jew, the history I inherited, and the future I am helping to build, all of it is contained within the declaration that Hashem is One.

Shema therefore moves us beyond ourselves. It is not about aligning the world with my preferences. It is about aligning my life with the one reality of Hashem. That is what it means to live Shema rather than simply recite it.

VII. The Broken Luchos and What the Aron Carried

This theme connects back to the Chet HaEgel and the breaking of the Luchos. At the end of the Torah, Rashi interprets Hashem's final praise of Moshe as approval for breaking the tablets: yasher koach sheshibarta, strength to you for having broken them. Moshe saw the Egel and understood that Klal Yisrael was not ready to receive the first Luchos in that moment.

But Jewish history did not end with the breaking. Moshe climbed the mountain again. Hashem forgave. A second set of Luchos was given. And Chazal teach that both the whole Luchos and the fragments of the first Luchos were placed together in the Aron. The Aron carried both brokenness and wholeness. That image speaks powerfully to us in the days after Tisha B'Av. We do not erase what was shattered. We carry it. We carry the Egel. We carry the destruction of both Batei Mikdash. We carry the expulsions and the Shoah and October 7. But the broken pieces do not travel alone. Beside them are the second Luchos, the testimony that teshuvah remains possible, that the covenant can be renewed, and that Hashem gives us the tools to climb the mountain again.

VIII. Four Generations and Thousands

The Aseres HaDibros makes a striking contrast that is easy to read past. The Torah states:

פֹּקֵד עֲוֹן אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים וְעַל שִׁלֵּשִׁים וְעַל רִבֵּעִים לְשֹׂנְאָי

"...remembering the premeditated sins of the fathers, adding their demerits to those of their descendants, up to the third and the fourth generation, for those who hate Me."

— Devarim 5:9

And then immediately:

וְעֹשֶׂה חֶסֶד לַאֲלָפִים לְאֹהֲבַי וּלְשֹׁמְרֵי מִצְוֹתָי

"But I am a God who shows kindness for at least two thousand generations to the descendants of those who love Me and who observe My commandments."

— Devarim 5:10

Rashi explains that the measure of goodness exceeds the measure of punishment by five hundred times. Punishment echoes across four generations. Goodness reaches at least two thousand. The contrast is not subtle. Torah places a real and bounded limit on the echo of sin, and against that limit sets an almost incomprehensible expansiveness of chesed.

This does not mean that sin is insignificant. National failures create real echoes. Chazal teach that later punishments retain some measure of the consequences of the Chet HaEgel. Brokenness can travel through generations. But Torah places a boundary around punishment, and that boundary is narrow compared to the expansiveness of chesed.

A parent who teaches a child Shema creates an echo that can reach thousands of generations. A teacher who enables a student to experience Torah as a living reality creates an echo. A soldier who protects another Jew creates an echo. A family that opens its home, performs chesed, learns, rebuilds, or chooses emunah inside suffering creates an echo. Hashem has given us the tools to build something that outlasts every destruction. The question is whether we will use them.

IX. Comfort Is Not Closure

Then comes the haftorah:

נַחֲמוּ נַחֲמוּ עַמִּי

"Comfort, comfort My people."

— Yeshayahu 40:1

This comfort does not deny the destruction. It does not pretend that nothing was broken or that no one was lost. Yeshayahu speaks to an exhausted people. Human beings are like grass that withers. Nations that appear invincible will not endure forever. Only the word of Hashem remains. Then the haftorah tells us:

שְׂאוּ מָרוֹם עֵינֵיכֶם וּרְאוּ מִי בָרָא אֵלֶּה

"Raise your eyes on high and see: Who created these?"

— Yeshayahu 40:26

Raise your eyes. Look upward. Remember who created the world, who directs history, and who knows every individual by name. That is nechamah. Not a declaration that the story is finished. Not a command to stop mourning before the mourning has done its work. Nechamah means that from within the suffering we rediscover the strength to continue. It means we remember that Hashem has not abandoned us. It means we recognize that an awakening from below, turning toward Hashem, draws a response from above, strengthening us beyond what we could achieve alone.

Yesterday we sat on the floor together. We cried and mourned the Beis HaMikdash together. When we confront our challenges together, when we say Shema together and sit around a Shabbos table together and perform all these beautiful things together, we are loving Hashem together and doing it for Hashem. That togetherness is itself part of the nechamah. Those who have oppressed us will not endure forever. The punishment has limits. The chesed does not.

X. We Are Still Writing

We are not yet delivering the final hesped of our generation. The story is still unfolding. We are still being called to teshuvah. We are still being asked to strengthen one another. We still carry the broken Luchos, but we also carry the second Luchos. We still bear the echoes of earlier failures, but we have the capacity to create goodness that will endure for thousands of generations.

Hashem wants us to succeed. Hashem has given us the tools: memory, Torah, chukim and mishpatim, the living edus of our teachers, the Aseres HaDibros, Shema, tefillin, mezuzah, teshuvah. We are supposed to become the third Beis HaMikdash. Each person who lives Torah honestly, each home that makes Hashem's presence felt, each teacher who transmits edus rather than just information, is building another stone in the structure we are meant to complete together.

Now we must raise our eyes, use what Hashem has given us, and continue building until the third Beis HaMikdash is no longer only something we see in our dreams and visions, but a physical reality in this world.

חזק ואחזק

Good Shabbos

Reflection Questions

• Tisha B'Av passed, but the story of our generation has not concluded. What is one specific response I am still being called to make, personally or communally, that I have not yet made?

• What is the difference between edus and information in my own Jewish life? Is there something I know intellectually but have not yet truly experienced? What would it take to cross that gap?

• Moshe speaks to people who were not at Sinai as though they were. What inherited experience of Klal Yisrael do I carry in my bones, and am I passing it to the next generation as living testimony or only as historical fact?

• The Aron carried both the whole Luchos and the broken fragments together. What brokenness am I carrying that I have tried to hide or discard, when it may actually belong beside what is whole?

• Goodness reaches thousands of generations; punishment is bounded to four. What echo am I creating right now, and what would it mean to build something whose positive ripple outlasts me?

• Nachamu does not mean the story is finished. Where do I need comfort that does not demand premature closure, and where am I being called to raise my eyes rather than remain fixed on the ground?
